claims.text: Brittle failure in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy emerges from a mechanism other than traditional chemical segregation or intermetallic precipitation.
High-strain-rate deformation induces severe dynamic grain refinement in the alloy.
Dynamic grain refinement increases the fraction of high-angle grain boundaries and triple junctions.
High-angle grain boundaries in CoCrFeMnNi have relatively high interfacial energy.
High-energy boundaries and triple junctions are prone to localized cohesive failure or decohesion.
Boundary and triple-junction decohesion can occur in solid-solution CoCrFeMnNi without significant segregation or phase separation.
High-energy boundaries and triple junctions facilitate local amorphization.
Interfacial decohesion or cavitation produced by the refined boundary network causes a ductile-to-brittle transition and loss of toughness.
The proposed test material is an initially coarse-grained, single-phase, compositionally complex alloy such as CoCrFeMnNi.
Single-phase FCC high- and medium-entropy alloys based on Al, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni can exhibit a rapid decrease in ductility between 400 and 800 degrees Celsius.
High-rate deformation at intermediate temperature will produce more grain refinement than low-rate deformation at room temperature.
High-rate, intermediate-temperature deformation will increase the high-angle grain-boundary and triple-junction fractions relative to the baseline.
High-rate, intermediate-temperature deformation will produce local amorphization, cavitation, or decohesion at boundaries and triple junctions.
The predicted microstructural changes will correlate with a marked loss of toughness.
At low strain rate and room temperature, the coarse-grained single-phase alloy remains ductile with minimal grain refinement and no significant boundary decohesion.
Using ultra-high vacuum or inert gas minimizes oxidation and other effects of chemically reactive environmental species.
Using ultra-high vacuum or inert gas ensures that segregation remains negligible during elevated-temperature deformation.
The brittle transition occurs only within temperature and strain-rate ranges sufficient to activate dynamic grain refinement.
At very low temperature or below a critical strain rate, grain-boundary decohesion will not be activated.

Failure to observe grain refinement, increased high-angle-boundary or triple-junction fraction, or interfacial decohesion under the high-rate condition would falsify the proposed causal mechanism even if toughness decreases.
